dn22:0.2: The Long Discourse about the Ways of Attending to Mindfulness
dn22:1.2: at one time the Fortunate One was dwelling amongst the Kurus near a market town of the Kurus named Kammāssadamma.
dn22:1.3: There the Fortunate One addressed the monks (saying):
dn22:1.5: “Monks!” “Venerable Sir!” those monks replied to the Fortunate One,
dn22:1.6: and the Fortunate One said this:
dn22:1.7: “This is a one-way path, monks, for the purification of beings, for the overcoming of grief and lamentation, for the extinction of pain and sorrow, for attaining the right way, for the direct realisation of Nibbāna, that is to say, the four ways of attending to mindfulness.
dn22:1.9: Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating (the nature of) the body in the body, ardent, fully aware, and mindful, after removing avarice and sorrow regarding the world.
dn22:1.10: He dwells contemplating (the nature of) feelings in feelings, ardent, fully aware, and mindful, after removing avarice and sorrow regarding the world.
dn22:1.11: He dwells contemplating (the nature of) the mind in the mind, ardent, fully aware, and mindful, after removing avarice and sorrow regarding the world.
dn22:1.12: He dwells contemplating (the nature of) things in (various) things, ardent, fully aware, and mindful, after removing avarice and sorrow regarding the world.
dn22:2.0.2: The Section about In-breathing and Out-breathing
dn22:2.1: And how, monks, does a monk dwell contemplating (the nature of) the body in the body?
dn22:2.2: Here, monks, a monk who has gone to the wilderness, or has gone to the root of a tree, or has gone to an empty place, sits down. After folding his legs crosswise, setting his body straight, and establishing mindfulness at the front,
dn22:2.3: being very mindful he breathes in, mindful he breathes out.
dn22:2.4: While breathing in long, he knows “I am breathing in long”, or, while breathing out long, he knows “I am breathing out long”;
dn22:2.5: or, while breathing in short, he knows “I am breathing in short”, or, while breathing out short, he knows “I am breathing out short”.
dn22:2.6: Experiencing the whole body I will breathe in, like this he trains, experiencing the whole body I will breathe out, like this he trains;
dn22:2.7: calming the bodily process I will breathe in, like this he trains, calming the bodily process I will breathe out, like this he trains.
dn22:2.8: Just as, monks, a clever turner or turner’s apprentice while making a long turn knows “I am making a long turn”, or, while making a short turn knows “I am making a short turn”,
dn22:2.9: just so, monks, a monk while breathing in long, knows “I am breathing in long”, or, while breathing out long, he knows “I am breathing out long”; or, while breathing in short, he knows “I am breathing in short”, or, while breathing out short, he knows “I am breathing out short”.
dn22:2.10: Experiencing the whole body I will breathe in, like this he trains, experiencing the whole body I will breathe out, like this he trains; calming the bodily process I will breathe in, like this he trains, calming the bodily process I will breathe out, like this he trains.
dn22:2.11: Thus he dwells contemplating (the nature of) the body in the body in regard to himself, or he dwells contemplating (the nature of) the body in the body in regard to others, or he dwells contemplating (the nature of) the body in the body in regard to himself and in regard to others,
dn22:2.12: or he dwells contemplating the nature of origination in the body, or he dwells contemplating the nature of dissolution in the body, or he dwells contemplating the nature of origination and dissolution in the body,
dn22:2.13: or else mindfulness that “there is a body” is established in him just as far as (is necessary for) a full measure of knowledge and a full measure of mindfulness, and he dwells independent, and without being attached to anything in the world.
dn22:2.14: In this way, monks, a monk dwells contemplating (the nature of) the body in the body.
dn22:2.15: The Section about In-breathing and Out-breathing is Finished

dn22:5.0: The Section about Applying the Mind to Repulsiveness
dn22:5.1: Moreover, monks, a monk in regard to this very body - from the sole of the feet upwards, from the hair of the head down, bounded by the skin, and full of manifold impurities - reflects (thus):
dn22:5.2: “There are in this body: hairs of the head, body hairs, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone-marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, pleura, spleen, lungs, intestines, mesentery, undigested food, excrement, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, spit, mucus, synovial fluid, urine.”
dn22:5.3: Just as though, monks, there were a bag open at both ends, full of various kinds of grain, such as: hill rice, white rice, mung beans, kidney beans, sesame seeds, chickpeas; and a man with good vision having opened it were to reflect (thus): “This is hill rice, this is white rice, these are mung beans, these are sesame seeds, these are chickpeas”;
dn22:5.4: even so, monks, a monk in regard to this very body - from the sole of the feet upwards, from the hair of the head down, bounded by the skin, and full of manifold impurities - reflects (thus):
dn22:5.5: “There are in this body, hairs of the head, body hairs, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone-marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, pleura, spleen, lungs, intestines, mesentery, undigested food, excrement, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, spit, mucus, synovial fluid, urine.”

dn22:11.1: And how, monks, does a monk dwell contemplating (the nature of) feelings in feelings?

dn22:11.3: or, when experiencing an unpleasant feeling he knows “I experience an unpleasant feeling”;
dn22:11.4: or, when experiencing a neither-unpleasant-nor-pleasant feeling he knows “I experience a neither-unpleasant-nor-pleasant feeling”.

dn22:11.7: or, when experiencing a sensual unpleasant feeling he knows “I experience a sensual unpleasant feeling”;

dn22:13.1: And how, monks, does a monk dwell contemplating (the nature of) things in (various) things?

dn22:13.3: And how, monks, does a monk dwell contemplating (the nature of) things in (various) things, in the five hindrances?
dn22:13.4: Here, monks, a monk having sensual desire in himself knows “there is sensual desire in myself”; or, not having sensual desire in himself he knows “there is no sensual desire in myself”. How there is an arising of sensual desire that has not arisen – that he knows; and how there is an abandonment of sensual desire that has arisen – that also he knows; and how there is a non-arising of abandoned sensual desire again in the future – that also he knows.
dn22:13.5: Having ill-will in himself he knows “there is ill-will in myself”; or, not having ill-will in himself he knows “there is no ill-will in myself”. How there is an arising of ill-will that has not arisen – that he knows; and how there is an abandonment of ill-will that has arisen – that also he knows; and how there is a non-arising of abandoned ill-will again in the future – that also he knows.
dn22:13.6: Having sloth and torpor in himself he knows “there is sloth and torpor in myself”; or, not having sloth and torpor in himself he knows “there is no sloth and torpor in myself”. dn22:17.1: Moreover, monks, a monk dwells contemplating (the nature of) things in (various) things, in the Four Noble Truths.
dn22:17.2: And how, monks, does a monk dwell contemplating (the nature of) things in (various) things, in the Four Noble Truths?
dn22:17.3: Here, monks, a monk knows as it really is “this is Suffering”, he knows as it really is “this is the Origination of Suffering”, he knows as it really is “this is the Cessation of Suffering”, he knows as it really is “this is the Practice Leading to the Cessation of Suffering”.
dn22:18.1: Now what, monks, is the Noble Truth of Suffering?
dn22:18.2: Birth is suffering also old age is suffering also death is suffering also grief, lamentation, pain, sorrow, and despair, is suffering also being joined to what is not liked is suffering, also being parted from what is liked is suffering, also not to obtain that which one longs for is suffering in brief, the five constituents (of mind and body) that provide fuel for attachment are suffering.
dn22:18.4: For the various beings in the various classes of beings (there is) birth, being born, appearing, turning up; the manifestation of the constituents (of mind and body), the acquisition of the sense spheres:
dn22:18.6: Now what, monks, is old age?
dn22:18.7: For the various beings in the various classes of beings there is old age, agedness, broken teeth, greying hair, and wrinkled skin; the dwindling away of the lifespan, the decay of the sense faculties:
dn22:18.8: this, monks, is called old age.
dn22:18.10: For the various beings in the various classes of beings there is a fall, a falling away, a breaking up, a disappearance, a dying, a death, a making of time; the break up of the constituents (of mind and body), the throwing off of the body; the cutting off of the life faculty:
dn22:18.13: For he who has, monks, some sort of misfortune or other, who is touched by some sort of painful thing or another, there is grief, grieving, the state of grieving, inner grief, great inner grief:
dn22:18.16: For he who has, monks, some sort of misfortune or other, who is touched by some sort of painful thing or another, there are laments, great laments, lamenting, great lamenting, the state of lamenting, the state of great lamentation:
dn22:18.19: That, monks, which is bodily pain, bodily disagreeableness, pain born of contact with the body, disagreeable feeling:
dn22:18.22: That, monks, which is mental pain, mental disagreeableness, pain born of contact with the mind, disagreeable feeling:
dn22:18.25: For he who has, monks, some sort of misfortune or other, who is touched by some sort of painful thing or another, there is desponding, despairing, the state of despondency, the state of despair:
dn22:18.27: And what, monks, is the suffering from being joined to what is not liked?
dn22:18.28: Here, for that one who has unwanted, unlovely, unpleasant forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, and thoughts; or, for that one who has those who do not desire his welfare, benefit, comfort and security - (and then) having meetings, assembly, connection, and interaction with them:
dn22:18.29: this, monks, is called the suffering from being joined to what is not liked.
dn22:18.30: And what, monks, is the suffering from being parted from what is liked?
dn22:18.31: Here, for that one who has wanted, lovely, pleasant forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, and thoughts; or, for that one who has those who do desire his welfare, benefit, comfort and security - mothers, or fathers, or brothers, or sisters, or friends, or companions, or blood relatives - (and then) not having meetings, assembly, connection, and interaction with them:
dn22:18.32: this, monks, is called the suffering from being parted from what is liked.
dn22:18.33: Now what, monks, is the suffering from not obtaining what one longs for?
dn22:18.34: To those beings subject to birth, monks, a longing like this arises:
dn22:18.35: “Oh, might we not be subject to birth, may birth not come to us!”
dn22:18.36: But that cannot be attained merely by longing for it:
dn22:18.37: this is the suffering from not obtaining what one longs for.
dn22:18.38: To those beings subject to old age, monks, a longing like this arises:
dn22:18.39: “Oh, might we not be subject to old age, may old age not come to us!”
dn22:18.40: But that cannot be attained merely by longing for it: this is the suffering from not obtaining what one longs for.
dn22:18.41: To those beings subject to sickness, monks, a longing like this arises: “Oh, might we not be subject to sickness, may sickness not come to us!”
dn22:18.42: But that cannot be attained merely by longing for it: this is the suffering from not obtaining what one longs for.
dn22:18.43: To those beings subject to death, monks, a longing like this arises: “Oh, might we not be subject to death, may death not come to us!”
dn22:18.44: But that cannot be attained merely by longing for it: this is the suffering from not obtaining what one longs for.
dn22:18.45: o To those beings subject to grief, lamentation, pain, sorrow, and despair, monks, a longing like this arises: “Oh, might we not be subject to grief, lamentation, pain, sorrow, and despair, may grief, lamentation, pain, sorrow, and despair, not come to us!”
dn22:18.46: But that cannot be attained merely by longing for it:
dn22:18.47: this is the suffering from not obtaining what one longs for.
dn22:18.48: Now what, monks, in brief, are the five constituents (of mind and body) that provide fuel for attachment which are suffering? They are as follows: the form constituent that is fuel for attachment
dn22:18.49: the feelings constituent that is fuel for attachment the perceptions constituent that is fuel for attachment the (mental) processes constituent that is fuel for attachment the consciousness constituent that is fuel for attachment.
dn22:18.50: These, monks, are called, in brief, the five constituents (of mind and body) that provide fuel for attachment which are suffering.
dn22:18.51: This, monks, is called the Noble Truth of Suffering.

dn22:21.1: Now what, monks, is the Noble Truth of the Practice Leading to the Cessation of Suffering?
dn22:21.2: It is this noble path with eight factors, as follows:
dn22:21.3: right view, right thought, right speech, right action, right livelihood right endeavour, right mindfulness, right concentration.
dn22:21.4: Now what, monks, is right view?
dn22:21.5: That, monks, which is knowledge about suffering knowledge about the origination of suffering knowledge about the cessation of suffering knowledge about the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
dn22:21.6: This, monks, is called right view.
dn22:21.7: Now what, monks, is right thought?
dn22:21.8: The thought of renunciation, the thought of good-will, the thought of non-violence.
dn22:21.9: This, monks, is called right thought.
dn22:21.10: Now what, monks, is right speech?
dn22:21.11: Refraining from false speech refraining from malicious speech refraining from rough speech refraining from frivolous talk.
dn22:21.12: This, monks, is called right speech.
dn22:21.13: Now what, monks, is right action?
dn22:21.14: Refraining from killing living creatures refraining from taking what has not been given refraining from sexual misconduct.
dn22:21.15: This, monks, is called right action.
dn22:21.16: Now what, monks, is right livelihood?
dn22:21.17: Here, monks, a noble disciple, having abandoned a wrong way of livelihood, makes his living by a right way of livelihood.
dn22:21.18: This, monks, is called right livelihood.
dn22:21.19: Now what, monks, is right endeavour?
dn22:21.20: o Here, monks, a monk regarding bad and unwholesome thoughts that have not yet arisen generates desire for the non-arising, (in this regard) he endeavours, instigates energy, exerts his mind, and makes an effort.
dn22:21.21: Regarding bad and unwholesome thoughts that have already arisen he generates desire for their abandonment, (in this regard) he endeavours, instigates energy, exerts his mind, and makes an effort.
dn22:21.22: He generates desire for the arising of wholesome thoughts that have not yet arisen, (in this regard) he endeavours, instigates energy, exerts his mind, and makes an effort.
dn22:21.23: o Regarding wholesome thoughts that have arisen generates desire for their endurance, persistence, multiplication, extension, development, and fulfilment, (in this regard) he endeavours, instigates energy, exerts his mind, and makes an effort.
dn22:21.24: This, monks, is called right endeavour.
dn22:21.25: Now what, monks, is right mindfulness?
dn22:21.26: Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating (the nature of) the body in the body, ardent, fully aware, and mindful, after removing avarice and sorrow regarding the world.
dn22:21.27: He dwells contemplating (the nature of) feelings in feelings, ardent, fully aware, and mindful, after removing avarice and sorrow regarding the world.
dn22:21.28: He dwells contemplating (the nature of) the mind in the mind, ardent, fully aware, and mindful, after removing avarice and sorrow regarding the world.
dn22:21.29: He dwells contemplating (the nature of) things in (various) things, ardent, fully aware, and mindful, after removing avarice and sorrow regarding the world.
dn22:21.30: This, monks, is called right mindfulness.
dn22:21.31: Now what, monks, is right concentration?
dn22:21.32: Here, monks, a monk, quite secluded from sense desires, secluded from unwholesome things, having thinking, reflection, and the happiness and joy born of seclusion, dwells having attained the first absorption.
dn22:21.33: With the calming down of thinking and reflection, with internal clarity, and one-pointedness of mind, being without thinking, without reflection, having the happiness and joy born of concentration, he dwells having attained the second absorption.
dn22:21.34: With the fading away of joy he dwells equanimous, mindful, fully aware, experiencing happiness through the body, about which the Noble Ones declare: “He dwells pleasantly, mindful, and equanimous,” he dwells having attained the third absorption.
dn22:21.35: Having abandoned pleasure, abandoned pain, and with the previous passing away of mental happiness and sorrow, without pain, without pleasure, and with complete purity of mindfulness owing to equanimity, he dwells having attained the fourth absorption.
dn22:21.36: This, monks, is called right concentration.
dn22:21.37: This, monks, is called the Noble Truth of the Practice Leading to the Cessation of Suffering.
dn22:21.38: Thus he dwells contemplating (the nature of) things in (various) things in regard to himself, or he dwells contemplating (the nature of) things in (various) things in regard to others, or he dwells contemplating (the nature of) things in (various) things in regard to himself and in regard to others,
dn22:21.39: or he dwells contemplating the nature of origination in things, or he dwells contemplating the nature of dissolution in things, or he dwells contemplating the nature of origination and dissolution in things,
dn22:21.40: or else mindfulness that “there are these (various) things” is established in him just as far as (is necessary for) a full measure of knowledge and a full measure of mindfulness, and he dwells independent, and without being attached to anything in the world.
dn22:21.41: In this way, monks, a monk dwells contemplating (the nature of) things in (various) things,
dn22:21.42: The Section about the Four Truths is Finished
